content.text: A chick grows into a chicken
The chicks are the young. The hen is an adult chicken.
The chick eats and drinks. Its body grows bigger and changes into an adult chicken.

elements.alt: A mother hen with her chicks on a concrete staircase, showcasing farm life.
elements.name: Photo slot

evidence.alt: A mother hen with her chicks on a concrete staircase, showcasing farm life.

slides.notes: Read the text aloud. Point to the chicks, then to the hen. Explain that young means an animal near the start of its life; adult means fully grown. This adult chicken is a hen. Introduce our case: this chick is small and fluffy. We will find out how it changes and what it needs to grow.

content.text: A lamb is a young sheep. As it grows, its body gets bigger and changes into an adult sheep.
A kitten is a young cat. A puppy is a young dog.
Young animals grow bigger. Their bodies change as they grow into adults.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: A table matches a lamb to a sheep, a kitten to a cat and a puppy to a dog.

slides.notes: Read each row from young to adult, pointing as you speak. A lamb does not become a different kind of animal: it is a young sheep. The names tell us whether the animal is young or adult. Explain the same idea for kitten and puppy.

content.text: Match each young animal to its grown-up.

slides.notes: Answers: puppy matches dog; lamb matches sheep; kitten matches cat. Each young animal grows into an adult of its own kind. Read all the words aloud before pupils match them together with the class. A wrong match suggests that the young-animal name is not secure. Return to that row in the table, then ask pupils to correct their match.

content.text: A chick changes as it grows
A hen forages with chicks. The chicks are young chickens.
Chicks grow into adult hens. Their bodies change as they grow.

elements.alt: A hen with chicks foraging on a farm. Captures domestic poultry in a natural setting.
elements.name: Photo slot

evidence.alt: A hen with chicks foraging on a farm. Captures domestic poultry in a natural setting.

slides.notes: Point first to the chick's small body and fluffy feathers. Then point to the hen's larger body and longer wing and tail feathers. Both are chickens, even though they look different. Growing is more than becoming a larger copy: parts of an animal's body can change too. Keep the comparison focused on features clearly visible in the photograph.

content.text: How does a small, fluffy chick change as it grows into a hen?
the adult has a larger body.
Grow longer wing and tail feathers

slides.notes: Show the first line and say that an explanation starts with what the young animal is like. Before revealing the second line, ask the class what happens to its size. Before revealing the final line, ask what changes about its feathers. Read the whole explanation together: the chick starts small and fluffy, grows bigger and develops longer wing and tail feathers. These changes explain why it does not look exactly like a tiny hen.

content.text: What are young animals always like compared with their adults?

slides.notes:
Young animals are younger than their adults, but they do not always look the same.
Answer: younger. Being young tells us about the animal's stage of life. Exactly the same is wrong: the chick and hen have different sizes and feathers. Bigger reverses the growth shown in our example. Fluffier treats a feature of our chick as a rule for every young animal. Read the options aloud and take an answer from every pupil. If pupils choose exactly the same, revisit the photograph and point to the different wing and tail feathers before moving on.

content.text: Young animals need care to grow
Their fluffy feathers show they are young.
Food helps chicks grow. Water helps their bodies work.
Chicks need air to breathe and warmth to stay well.

elements.alt: Yellow chicks gathered in a pen under sunlight, highlighting their fluffy feathers.
elements.name: Photo slot

evidence.alt: Yellow chicks gathered in a pen under sunlight, highlighting their fluffy feathers.

slides.notes: Point to the food, drinking water and protective enclosure. Explain that this is a home made to care for young chicks. Its heat source provides warmth. Air is around the chicks even though we cannot see it. Food supports growth, and animals also need water and air to live. Different young animals need suitable food: chicks eat chick food, while young kittens drink their mother's milk. Adults caring for young animals must provide a safe home and enough warmth.

content.text: Say or write a short answer for each task.
1: Match a lamb to its adult and say how you know.
2: Explain how a kitten changes as it grows into a cat.
3: Use feathers to explain why a fluffy chick is not exactly like a small hen.
4: A chick has food; say which adult it becomes and how water, air, warmth and a safe home help it grow.

slides.notes: Read each task aloud, then let pupils answer independently using speech, drawing with labels or writing. Answers: 1. A lamb is a young sheep. 2. A kitten grows bigger as it becomes an adult cat. 3. A chick has fluffy feathers, but a small hen has longer wing and tail feathers. This shows the chick is not just a small hen: its feathers change as it grows into an adult. 4. A chick grows into an adult chicken. It needs water, air, warmth and a safe home to live and grow. Food alone is not enough. This settles our original chick case: it grows into an adult chicken, changes in size and feathers, and needs care to live and grow. Harder challenge: Would chick food be the right food for a very young kitten? Explain. Answer: No. A very young kitten needs its mother’s milk, so young animals do not all need the same food.
